name: Taoism
line: Move with the way of things, not against it.

quote.text: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.

quotes.text: The highest good is like water. Water benefits all things and does not contend.
The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao.
In the pursuit of learning, every day something is acquired. In the pursuit of Tao, every day something is dropped.
quotes.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 48, trans. Gia-fu Feng and Jane English

quotes.text: Shape clay into a vessel: it is the space within that makes it useful.
Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, yet nothing is better at overcoming the hard and strong.
Knowing others is intelligence; knowing yourself is true wisdom.
quotes.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 33, trans. Gia-fu Feng and Jane English

words.usage: The source and pattern of everything. Also written Tao.

words.meaning: Virtue; the power of the Way in a particular thing
words.usage: What a thing is when nothing interferes with it.
Not doing nothing: doing nothing that goes against the grain.
Literally "self-so". How things are when left to be themselves.
Plain wood before it is cut: your original simplicity.
What moves in the body and between heaven and earth.

words.meaning: The shaded and the sunlit; complementary opposites
words.usage: Each contains the seed of the other and turns into it.
The turning of yin and yang, drawn as the familiar divided circle.
The stillness that movement comes out of.
The empty hub that lets the wheel turn.
Chapter 40: returning is the movement of the Way.
The living are soft and supple; the dead are stiff and hard.
The favourite image of the Way: low, soft and unstoppable.
One word for what English splits into thinking and feeling.
Zhuangzi: listen not with the ear or the mind but with qi, which is empty and waits.
Dropping body, knowledge and self until you merge with the great thoroughfare.
The title of the first chapter of the Zhuangzi.
Everything that exists.
Not a place above but the order things follow.
Zhuangzi’s name for someone no longer at odds with the Way.
The character combines "person" and "mountain".
An ordained ritual specialist of the living religion.
The word also means to observe.
The old arts of health: breath, movement, diet, rest.
A modern umbrella term for very old exercises.
A martial art practiced slowly as moving meditation.
The centre below the navel where breath is gathered.
Meditation described in the language of the alchemist’s furnace.
Wood, fire, earth, metal, water: a cycle, not a list of substances.
First of the three treasures in chapter 67.
Second of the three treasures.
Different things fitting together without becoming the same.

practices.name: Morning qigong
practices.instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, arms loose. Breathe low into the belly for a minute. Then move slowly through a simple set, such as the Eight Pieces of Brocade: raise the hands to hold up the sky, draw the bow to each side, lift one arm at a time, look back over each shoulder, sway head and tail, fold forward, and finish by rubbing the hands warm. Go slowly and stop if anything hurts.
practices.why: Yangsheng, nourishing life, is one of the oldest strands of Daoist practice. The body is not an obstacle to the Way; it is where you meet it.
variations: Stand still for ten minutes in the holding-the-tree posture.
Follow a tai chi short form.
Practise outdoors, facing the morning light.

practices.name: Standing like a tree
practices.instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and knees slightly soft. Let the arms rise as if holding a large ball at chest height. Relax the shoulders, drop the tailbone, breathe low into the belly. Stand until the legs warm and the mind quiets. Stop if you feel pain or dizziness; this is a gentle posture, not an endurance test.
practices.why: Standing practice (zhan zhuang) is a common qigong exercise. It trains rootedness and doing nothing on purpose, which is close to the spirit of wu wei.
variations: Stand by a tree and imitate it.
Three minutes only.
Lean your back against a wall if balance is hard.

practices.name: Wake the body
practices.instructions: Before you stand up, stretch like a cat: arms overhead, toes pointed, a long slow yawn. Roll to one side, then the other, and pull each knee in. Sit up slowly, circle your shoulders and neck, then stand. Move as if you had all day. A body that is woken gently stays soft for hours.
practices.why: Daoist health practice begins with the body: stretch, breathe, warm up the joints. Animals do this naturally. The old texts copy the stretch of the bear and the bird.
variations: Stretch until the first yawn comes by itself.
Stretch in a patch of sun.
Add a slow turn of the head from side to side.

practices.name: Drink like water
practices.instructions: Pour a cup of warm water. Hold it in both hands and drink it slowly in small sips, feeling the warmth travel down. Think of water as Laozi did: soft, patient, taking the lowest place, and yet wearing away stone. Ask where in your day you could be more like water.
practices.why: Chapter 8 of the Tao Te Ching says the highest good is like water: it benefits all things and does not compete. Warm water is also the everyday drink of much of China.
variations: Add a slice of ginger.
Pour it into your favourite cup.
Drink it standing by a window.

practices.name: Leave one thing alone
practices.instructions: Choose one thing you usually push at: a problem, a person, a result. Today, leave it alone. Take your hands off it and do not fix, hurry or manage it. Write one line on what you will not do. Then see what happens. Often, something moves on its own, and you learn how much of your force was only noise.
practices.why: Wu wei, effortless action, does not mean doing nothing. It means not forcing. Laozi says the sage acts without strain and everything gets done.
variations: Choose a small thing, such as a kettle that will boil by itself.
Pick a worry and decide to wait a day.
Notice each time you start to push, and soften.

practices.name: Warm hands, bright eyes
practices.instructions: Rub your palms together fast until they are hot. Place them gently over your closed eyes and rest for ten breaths. Then rub your hands over your face from the chin up, like washing without water. A few breaths of this wakes the eyes and face, and it is a pleasant way to start the day.
practices.why: Rubbing the hands and face is a standard opening in many qigong sets. It is a self-massage that says good morning to the senses.
variations: Rub your ears and the back of your neck too.
Do it again before you start work.
Do it by a window and open your eyes on the view.

practices.name: Walk without a goal
practices.instructions: Leave without a destination, a step count or headphones. At each corner take whichever way draws you. Walk at the speed at which you can still notice things. If you find yourself planning the route, stop, look around and begin again.
practices.why: Zhuangzi’s first chapter is called Free and Easy Wandering. Usefulness and purpose, he suggests, are how the big tree gets cut down.
variations: Follow water: a stream, a canal, a shoreline.
Wander one small area very slowly.
Walk in rain if it is raining.

practices.name: Tea, slowly
practices.instructions: Use loose leaves and a small pot or lidded cup. Warm the vessel, rinse the leaves with a quick pour, then steep briefly and pour it all out into the cup. Smell it before you drink. Make three or four short infusions and notice how each one differs.
practices.why: Gongfu tea means tea made with skill and time. It is a lesson in small adjustments, and in not rushing a thing that has its own pace.
variations: Drink the first cup in silence.
Share the pot with one other person.
Brew the same leaf every day and track how it changes.

practices.name: Do something useless
practices.instructions: Spend fifteen minutes on something with no use: draw a doodle, skip stones, lie on the grass, watch an ant. Do not tell yourself it will relax you or make you better. Just do it for its own sake. If a guilty voice says you should be productive, tell it that the useless tree lived to a great age.
practices.why: Zhuangzi tells of a huge gnarled tree no carpenter would cut, because it was useless, and so it lived for centuries. Doing a little useless thing keeps a corner of life free.
variations: Do it with a child.
Do something useless for ten minutes outdoors.
Make something that has no purpose and give it away.

practices.name: Take the lower place
practices.instructions: Today, take the lower place somewhere small: the last seat in the row, the last turn in the queue, the second word in the conversation. Do it lightly, not as a martyr. Notice how it feels, and what you hear from there that you could not hear from the front. Laozi says the sea is king of rivers because it lies below them.
practices.why: The Tao Te Ching praises the low: the sea, the valley, the female, water. To yield is not to lose. It is to leave room for everything else to come to you.
variations: Let someone else decide where to eat.
Give your seat or place in a queue.
Listen for one more minute before you speak.

practices.name: Sit by water
practices.instructions: Find water, a river, a pond, a fountain, even a tap running into a bowl, and sit beside it for ten minutes. Watch how it goes around stones, fills each hollow and does not push. Ask what it is doing that you are not. Leave a little more fluid than you came.
practices.why: Water is the Daoist teacher: yielding and yet unstoppable, taking the shape of any vessel. Chapter 78 says nothing is softer than water, and nothing beats it at wearing down the hard.
variations: Sit with your hand in the water.
Sit by the sea or a river if you can.
Listen to rain on a window and do nothing else.

practices.name: Taste the season
practices.instructions: Eat something that is in season where you live, a fruit, a root, a leaf, and eat it slowly, with nothing added. Ask what time of year it is by the taste. The Daoist calendar divides the year into twenty-four solar terms, each with its own foods. Warm food in the cold months, light food in the heat.
practices.why: Chinese tradition, and Daoist health practice in particular, ties eating to the twenty-four solar terms. It is a way of living inside the year, not above it.
variations: Find out which solar term it is and what to eat.
Visit a market and buy only what is in season.
Share it with someone.

practices.name: Observe the sky
practices.instructions: Go outside or to an open window. Look up for ten minutes. Note the phase of the moon, the wind, the temperature, what the clouds are doing. Do not photograph it. If you like, write one line afterwards.
practices.why: The old Daoists were sky-watchers and calendar-makers. To follow the Way you first have to notice which way things are moving.
variations: Learn tonight’s moon phase by name.
Note which of the twenty-four solar terms you are in.
Watch the same patch of sky at the same time all week.

practices.name: Sit and forget
practices.instructions: Sit comfortably and let the day fall away: the tasks, the faces, the voices. When a thought arrives, let it pass like a cloud. Do not try to be empty. Simply forget, bit by bit, the self that has been busy all day. After ten minutes, notice how much lighter you are.
practices.why: Zhuangzi describes zuowang, sitting and forgetting: dropping limbs, dismissing intelligence, merging with the great thoroughfare. It is the Daoist counterpart of quiet sitting.
variations: Sit by an open window.
Sit with a cup of warm water.
Sit for three minutes if ten is too many.

practices.name: Make space
practices.instructions: Choose a shelf, a drawer or a corner and take something out of it. Then another. Leave the space emptier than before. Look at it. Laozi says that a pot is useful because of the hollow in it, and a room because of its doors and windows. Notice what the empty space does for the things left.
practices.why: Chapter 11 of the Tao Te Ching: what is there gives profit, but what is not there gives use. Emptiness is not a lack. It is what makes things work.
variations: Leave one wall bare.
Clear one surface and leave it empty on purpose.
Leave ten minutes of your calendar free and protect it.

practices.name: One brushstroke
practices.instructions: Take a brush, a pen or even a finger dipped in water, and make one single stroke on a sheet of paper or a flat stone: a line, a curve, a circle. Do it in one breath. Look at it, then make another. Do not correct. Chinese painters say the brush reveals the mind. See which mind you brought.
practices.why: Daoist-influenced painters sought spontaneity, ziran. A single stroke made in one breath is a small, enjoyable training in letting things be as they are.
variations: Use water on a dark stone and watch it dry.
Draw the shape of a mountain in three strokes.
Write the character for water, shui.

practices.name: Warm feet, quiet mind
practices.instructions: Fill a basin with comfortably warm water and soak your feet for fifteen minutes. Sit with your back supported, breathe low into the belly, and let the warmth travel up. Add a pinch of salt or a slice of ginger if you like. Dry slowly and go straight to bed. It is an old, cheap pleasure.
practices.why: Foot soaking is a common practice in Chinese health care, said to draw energy downward and calm the head. Many people simply find it a delicious way to end the day.
variations: Do it while listening to quiet music.
Do it with a cup of chrysanthemum tea.
Do it with someone you love, side by side.

practices.name: The butterfly question
practices.instructions: Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, and woke not knowing if he was a man who had dreamed it or a butterfly dreaming it was a man. Write down one thing today that felt solid and then, in a different light, felt like a dream. Let the question stand. You do not need an answer to sleep well.
practices.why: The butterfly dream is the best-known story in the Zhuangzi. It is a gentle push away from certainty, and a good last thought for the day.
variations: Write about a dream you had last night.
Write what you would be if you were not you.
Tell the story to someone and ask what they think.

practices.name: Walk under the full moon
practices.instructions: On a night near the full moon, walk somewhere quiet and let the light be enough. Many observances in the Chinese lunar calendar fall on the first and fifteenth days of the month. Walk slowly, with nothing in your hands. Stop and look up at least once. Come home and drink something warm.
practices.why: The lunar calendar frames many Daoist observances, and walking by moonlight is a Chinese poet’s pleasure from the Tang onward. It is an easy way to feel the month turning.
variations: Go with one friend and say little.
Walk by water so the moon shines on it.
Write down one line of what you noticed.

practices.name: Climb to a high place
practices.instructions: Climb a hill, a tower or the top of a building. On the Double Ninth, people climb to a high place, drink chrysanthemum tea and honour their elders. Take your time, rest when you want to, and sit at the top for a while. Look at what you walked through. Come down a little lighter.
practices.why: Daoist temples sit on peaks, and the climb is part of the visit. Climbing to high places is the custom of the Double Ninth, and poets have written about it for two thousand years.
variations: Take someone older, at their pace.
Take a flask of chrysanthemum tea.
Climb a hill you can see from your window.

immersePlan.name: Read three chapters of the Tao Te Ching
immersePlan.text: Open the Tao Te Ching anywhere and read three chapters slowly. They are short. Choose the line that bothers you most, and sit with it for a few minutes before you move on.

immersePlan.name: Read a story from the Zhuangzi
immersePlan.text: Read one of the stories from the Inner Chapters: the butcher whose knife never dulls, the useless tree, the butterfly dream. Tell it to someone in your own words later today.

immersePlan.name: Read a poem by Hanshan
immersePlan.text: Read a few poems by Hanshan, the recluse who wrote on rocks and laughed at visitors. Choose one and read it aloud. Notice how far a plain voice can go.

immersePlan.name: Watch hermits in the mountains
immersePlan.text: Watch the film about hermits in the Zhongnan Mountains. They are mostly Buddhist, in the range where Daoists also live. Notice how much time they spend on ordinary tasks, and what they say about solitude.

immersePlan.name: Watch Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
immersePlan.text: Put on Ang Lee’s film of Wudang swordsmanship and the cost of holding on. Watch for the moments when softness beats force, and for the characters who cannot let go.

immersePlan.name: Watch Tai Chi Master
immersePlan.text: Watch the kung fu telling of the Zhang Sanfeng legend, in which yielding defeats force. Enjoy it as a film, then try standing very still for one minute and see how much strength it takes.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Flowing Water on the guqin
immersePlan.text: Play Guan Pinghu’s Flowing Water, seven strings and a great deal of silence. It was sent into space on the Voyager records. Listen with your eyes closed, and follow the pauses as much as the notes.

immersePlan.name: Listen to In Our Time on Daoism
immersePlan.text: Put on the programme where scholars discuss the texts, the religion and the difference between them. Listen on a walk, and note one thing that surprised you.

immersePlan.name: Hear the scholar’s instruments
immersePlan.text: Play a recording of guqin zither with xiao bamboo flute, the scholar’s instruments. Make a cup of tea, sit and do nothing else for ten minutes.

immersePlan.name: Look at Early Spring by Guo Xi
immersePlan.text: Look at the great mountain painting of 1072, a mountain that seems to breathe. Find the small figures first, then follow the mists up. Spend five minutes before you leave it.

immersePlan.name: Find the travellers
immersePlan.text: Look at Fan Kuan’s monumental landscape and find the travellers. They are very small. Ask what the painting is telling you about your place in the picture.

immersePlan.name: Look at a scholar’s rock
immersePlan.text: Look for photographs of a gongshi, a scholar’s rock, chosen and not carved. Then walk outside and choose a stone that has its own character. Hold it, look at it, put it somewhere you will see it.

immersePlan.name: Make a pot of congee
immersePlan.text: Simmer a cup of rice in eight cups of water until it is soft and creamy, with a pinch of salt. Add ginger or scallion and serve warm. Plain, easy on the body, and good on any day you feel run down.

immersePlan.name: Steam what is in season
immersePlan.text: Steam whatever vegetables are in season until just tender and barely season them. Taste each separately. Ask what the vegetable would say if it could speak.

immersePlan.name: Braise tofu and mushrooms
immersePlan.text: Braise tofu and mushrooms simply with a little soy sauce and ginger, as in monastery kitchens across China. Eat slowly with rice and notice how few things you need.

immersePlan.name: Brew oolong in several short steeps
immersePlan.text: Brew oolong in a small pot or cup: steep for thirty seconds, pour out, steep again for a little longer. Taste how each infusion differs. Stop when the flavour fades.

immersePlan.name: Drink pu-erh, dark and earthy
immersePlan.text: Rinse the pu-erh leaves with a quick pour, then steep briefly. It is dark, earthy and settling. Drink it with a plain biscuit and sit for a few minutes after you finish.

immersePlan.name: Brew chrysanthemum tea
immersePlan.text: Put a few dried chrysanthemum flowers in a glass cup and pour hot water over them. Watch them open. It was Tao Yuanming’s flower, and it is cooling in warm weather. Drink it slowly.

immersePlan.name: Practise at first light
immersePlan.text: In parks across China, people practise tai chi and qigong at first light. Today, take your own morning movement outdoors, even for five minutes. Do what you know, however simple.

immersePlan.name: Eat for the season
immersePlan.text: Chinese tradition eats by the twenty-four solar terms: warm food in winter, light food in summer. Plan one meal today that fits the weather outside. Notice how it feels to match the day.

immersePlan.name: Leave space on purpose
immersePlan.text: Chapter 11 says the empty part is what makes a thing useful. Today, leave a gap: a free half hour, an empty corner of a page, a pause before answering. Notice what it lets in.

immersePlan.name: Play Chinese chess
immersePlan.text: Play xiangqi, the Chinese chess in which two armies face each other across a river. Learn the basic moves, then play a short game. Notice how patience and tempo matter.

immersePlan.name: Play weiqi, known as Go
immersePlan.text: Play a short game of Go, which began in China. Place a stone, then another, and see how the board fills. Do not try to win each local fight. Think about balance and territory.

immersePlan.name: Play a little of Black Myth: Wukong
immersePlan.text: If you have the game, play for twenty minutes and look for the Taoist and Buddhist imagery from Journey to the West. If not, read a short summary of that story and imagine the world it describes.

immersePlan.name: Light a lantern for the first full moon
immersePlan.text: The Lantern Festival marks the first full moon of the lunar year. Make or buy a small paper lantern, or light a candle in a jar, and sit with it for ten minutes. Share it with someone, or simply look.

immersePlan.name: Keep the Double Ninth
immersePlan.text: On the ninth day of the ninth lunar month, people climb to a high place, drink chrysanthemum tea and honour their elders. Do any one of those three today, or ring an older relative.

immersePlan.name: Visit the Wudang Mountains by photograph
immersePlan.text: Look up pictures of the Wudang Mountains, peaks crowded with Daoist palaces and temples from the Ming dynasty. Find the one that draws you most, and imagine the climb.

immersePlan.name: Try wu wei on one task
immersePlan.text: Wu wei is effortless action, not forcing. Pick one task and do it with half the effort you usually give. Let the pace, the angle and the tool do their share. Notice what actually needed force.

immersePlan.name: Look for ziran
immersePlan.text: Ziran means so of itself, naturalness. Walk for ten minutes and look for things that are exactly as they are: a stone, a puddle, a weed in a crack. Say ziran quietly each time you find one.

immersePlan.name: Think of the uncarved block
immersePlan.text: Pu is the uncarved block: simplicity before shaping. Pick one thing in your life you have over-decorated, a plan, a room, a sentence, and strip it back by one layer.

rules.why: Chapter 30 warns that force is followed by loss of strength: what is pushed against the Way does not last. Try another angle, or a nap.
Hurry is a way of being absent from where you are. Walk as if you had already arrived.

rules.text: Spend part of the day outside
rules.why: The texts take their images from water, valleys, weather and trees. Go and check the originals.
Chapter 23: to talk little is natural, and a whirlwind does not last the whole morning. Leave the last sentence unsaid and see what happens.
Chapter 66: rivers and seas rule the hundred valleys because they lie below them. Let someone else go first, sit last, speak second.
Chapter 9: better to stop in time than to fill to the brim. Find the point where one more is one too many.

read.title: Tao Te Ching
read.creator: Laozi, trans. D. C. Lau
read.why: Eighty-one short chapters. A careful, scholarly translation.

read.title: Lao Tzu: Tao Te Ching
read.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
read.why: A poet’s rendering made with a sinologist: plain, dry and funny.

read.title: Zhuangzi: The Complete Writings
read.creator: trans. Brook Ziporyn
read.why: Butterflies, butchers, useless trees. Start with the seven Inner Chapters.

read.title: The Book of Lieh-tzu
read.creator: trans. A. C. Graham
read.why: Tales of the third classic, lighter and stranger than the other two.

read.title: Cold Mountain Poems
read.creator: Hanshan, trans. Red Pine
read.why: A recluse who wrote on rocks and laughed at visitors.

read.title: Selected Poems
read.creator: Tao Yuanming
read.why: The official who quit to grow chrysanthemums. The model for every later hermit poet.

read.title: Taoism: An Essential Guide
read.creator: Eva Wong
read.why: A practitioner’s map of the schools, from philosophy to ritual and alchemy.

read.title: Tao: The Watercourse Way
read.creator: Alan Watts
read.why: A Western popular account. Enjoyable, and to be read as one man’s view.

watch.title: Amongst White Clouds
watch.creator: Edward A. Burger
watch.why: Hermits in the Zhongnan Mountains. Mostly Buddhist, in the range Daoist recluses made famous.

watch.title: Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
watch.creator: Ang Lee
watch.why: Wudang swordsmanship and the cost of holding on.

watch.title: Tai Chi Master
watch.creator: Yuen Woo-ping
watch.why: A kung fu telling of the Zhang Sanfeng legend: softness defeats force.

listen.title: Flowing Water (Liu Shui)
listen.creator: Guan Pinghu, guqin
listen.why: Seven strings and a great deal of silence. Sent into space on the Voyager Golden Record.

listen.title: In Our Time: Daoism
listen.creator: BBC Radio 4, Melvyn Bragg
listen.why: Scholars on the texts, the religion and the difference between them.

listen.title: Guqin and xiao duets
listen.creator: Any traditional recording
listen.why: Zither and bamboo flute: the scholar’s instruments.

listen.title: Wudang Daoist ritual music
listen.creator: Temple recordings
listen.why: Chant, bells and drums from the mountain monasteries.

art.title: Early Spring
art.creator: Guo Xi
art.why: A mountain that seems to breathe. National Palace Museum, Taipei.

art.title: Travelers Among Mountains and Streams
art.creator: Fan Kuan
art.why: Find the travelers. They are very small.

art.title: Immortal in Splashed Ink
art.creator: Liang Kai
art.why: A drunken sage in a dozen wet strokes.

art.title: Laozi Riding an Ox
art.creator: Zhang Lu
art.why: The old man leaving through the western pass.

art.title: Scholar’s rocks
art.creator: Gongshi
art.why: Stones chosen, not carved. Look for one in a museum or a riverbed.

eat.title: Congee
eat.creator: Rice porridge
eat.why: Plain, warm and easy on the body. Add ginger or scallion.

eat.title: Steamed seasonal vegetables
eat.creator: Whatever is growing now
eat.why: Barely seasoned, so you can taste the season.

eat.title: Noodles in clear broth
eat.creator: With greens
eat.why: A meal that asks for very little.

drink.title: Chrysanthemum tea
drink.creator: Dried flowers in hot water
drink.why: Tao Yuanming’s flower. Cooling in warm weather.

drink.title: Warm water
drink.creator: Plain
drink.why: The everyday drink of much of China.

customs.title: Practice at dawn
customs.creator: Parks across China
customs.why: Tai chi and qigong in the park at first light is a living custom.

customs.title: Eat with the seasons
customs.creator: The twenty-four solar terms
customs.why: Warm food in winter, light food in summer.

customs.title: Leave space
customs.creator: In rooms, paintings and plans
customs.why: Chapter 11: the empty part is what makes the thing useful.

customs.title: Go to the mountains
customs.creator: Wudang, Hua, Tai
customs.why: Daoist temples sit on peaks. The climb is part of the visit.

customs.title: Offer incense
customs.creator: At a Daoist temple
customs.why: Three sticks, held in both hands. Follow what others do and ask if unsure.

customs.title: Follow the lunar calendar
customs.creator: New and full moon
customs.why: Many observances fall on the first and fifteenth day of the lunar month.

games.title: Xiangqi
games.creator: Board game · China
games.year: current form since the Song dynasty
games.why: Chinese chess. Two armies face each other across a river, and the generals may never see each other down an open file.

games.title: Weiqi
games.creator: Board game · China
games.why: The game known in the West as Go, born in China. Players are told not to fight for every stone: yield here to gain there.

games.title: Black Myth: Wukong
games.creator: Video game · Game Science
games.why: An action game after Journey to the West. Its world is full of Taoist immortals, alchemy furnaces and temples modelled on real sites in Shanxi.

festivals.title: Lantern Festival
festivals.creator: 15th day of the first lunar month
festivals.why: The first full moon of the year, kept as the birthday of the Heavenly Official who grants blessings. Lanterns, riddles and sweet rice balls.

festivals.title: Qingming
festivals.creator: Early April
festivals.why: The day of clear brightness. Families sweep the graves of their ancestors and walk out to see the spring.

festivals.title: Laozi’s birthday
festivals.creator: 15th day of the second lunar month
festivals.why: Temples honour Laozi as the Supreme Old Lord with offerings and readings of the Tao Te Ching.

festivals.title: Double Ninth
festivals.creator: 9th day of the ninth lunar month
festivals.why: A day for climbing to a high place, drinking chrysanthemum wine and honouring elders.

places.title: Wudang Mountains
places.creator: Hubei, China
places.why: Peaks covered in Taoist palaces and temples from the Ming dynasty, and the legendary home of the internal martial arts. A World Heritage Site.

places.title: White Cloud Temple
places.creator: Beijing, China
places.why: Chief temple of the Complete Reality school and seat of the Chinese Taoist Association. Monks live and study here.

places.title: Mount Tai
places.creator: Shandong, China
places.why: The eastern sacred mountain. Emperors climbed it to report to Heaven, and pilgrims still take the stone stairs to see the sunrise.

places.title: Louguantai
places.creator: Zhouzhi, Shaanxi, China
places.why: By tradition the pass where the gatekeeper Yin Xi asked Laozi to write down his teaching before he left for the west.

places.title: Mount Longhu
places.creator: Jiangxi, China
places.why: Dragon and Tiger Mountain, ancestral home of the Celestial Masters, with the river and red cliffs below.

ethics.title: Three treasures
ethics.text: Chapter 67: compassion, frugality, and not daring to be first in the world. From compassion comes courage; from frugality, generosity; from humility, leadership.
ethics.practice: Let someone else go first today, in a queue or in a conversation.

ethics.title: Be like water
ethics.text: Water gives life to everything and does not compete. It settles in the low places people avoid, and so it is close to the Way.
ethics.practice: In one disagreement, look for the way around instead of the way through.

ethics.title: Do not meddle
ethics.text: Govern a large country as you would cook a small fish: do not keep poking it. Much harm is done by fixing what was not broken.
ethics.practice: Resist improving one thing today that is working well enough.

ethics.title: Know when to stop
ethics.text: To know what is enough is to be rich. Disaster comes from not knowing when to stop.
ethics.practice: End one activity today while it is still going well.

ethics.title: No contention
ethics.text: Because the sage does not contend, no one under heaven can contend with them.
ethics.practice: Let one small provocation pass without reply.

ethics.title: Requite injury with virtue
ethics.text: Chapter 63: answer hostility with kindness and deal with the difficult while it is still easy.
ethics.practice: Do one small kindness for someone who has been cold to you.

philosophy.title: Wu wei
philosophy.text: Act without forcing. The best action fits the situation so well that it looks like no action at all, like a cook whose knife finds the gaps between the joints.
philosophy.practice: Find the easiest true way to do today’s hardest task.

philosophy.title: The uncarved block
philosophy.text: Return to simplicity. The more a thing is cut, named and polished, the further it moves from what it was.
philosophy.practice: Do one thing today without optimising it.

philosophy.title: Yin and yang
philosophy.text: Opposites create and complete each other: difficult and easy, long and short, before and after. Hold both and the turning makes sense.
philosophy.practice: When something goes badly, ask what it is turning into.

philosophy.title: Usefulness of emptiness
philosophy.text: Thirty spokes share one hub; the empty centre makes the wheel work. Doors and windows are what make a room.
philosophy.practice: Leave one hour of today unplanned and guard it.

philosophy.title: Return
philosophy.text: Returning is the movement of the Way. Things grow, flourish and go back to the root. Going back to the root is called stillness.
philosophy.practice: Sit for five minutes and do nothing whatever.

philosophy.title: The useless tree
philosophy.text: Zhuangzi: the gnarled tree no carpenter wants is the one that lives out its years. Usefulness is not the only measure of a life.
philosophy.practice: Spend twenty minutes on something with no purpose.

philosophy.title: Soft overcomes hard
philosophy.text: The tongue outlasts the teeth. What yields, endures; what is rigid, breaks.
philosophy.practice: In your body, find one place you are bracing, and let it go.

philosophy.title: The butterfly dream
philosophy.text: Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly, and on waking did not know which was the dreamer. Certainty about who you are may be the last thing to loosen.
philosophy.practice: Hold one opinion about yourself a little more lightly today.

philosophy.title: The Way cannot be named
philosophy.text: Any description of the Way is a finger, not the moon. Words are useful as long as you do not mistake them for the thing.
philosophy.practice: Notice one thing today that you cannot put into words. Leave it unsaid.

philosophy.title: Knowing enough
philosophy.text: There is no greater misfortune than not knowing what is enough.
philosophy.practice: Before buying or adding anything, ask what you would remove.

journal: Where did you force something today? Where did you yield?
What happened when you stopped trying?
What in nature held your attention?
Where could you do less and get more?
What did water teach you?
What was enough today?
What did you carry that you could set down?
Where did you rush, and what did rushing cost?
What went well without your interference?
Which opposite did you meet today, and how were the two connected?
What empty space made something else possible?
When did you say more than was needed?
What is growing now, and what is going back to the root?
Where did softness work better than strength?
What did you notice on your walk that you did not go looking for?
What would you do if you did not need to be useful?
Which desire today was really yours?
What did the sky do tonight?
Where did you take the higher place when the lower would have served?
What are you gripping? What would happen if you opened your hand?
What did the tea taste like, cup by cup?
What did you leave unimproved?
What part of your day followed the season?
Where did you contend, and with whom, and why?
What happened in your body during qigong?
What can you not name about today?
What turned into its opposite?
When were you most at ease, and what were you doing?
What would be simpler?
Describe today as weather.
reflect: What changed when you stopped pushing?
Which practice changed you the most, and why?
Where did you resist, and what was the resistance protecting?
What have you removed from your days that you do not miss?
What does "enough" look like to you now?
What will you keep doing, without effort?

intro: Taoism, or Daoism, is the Chinese tradition of living in accord with the Dao, the Way: the source, pattern and flow of everything that exists. Its advice can sound like doing less. It is closer to say: stop working against the grain.

It rests on two books. The Tao Te Ching, attributed to an old archivist called Laozi, is eighty-one brief chapters of paradox: the soft overcomes the hard, the empty is useful, the best ruler is barely noticed. The Zhuangzi, named after a fourth-century BCE writer of great wit, makes the same case with stories: a cook whose knife never dulls because it finds the spaces between the joints, a tree so gnarled that no carpenter cuts it down, a man who dreams he is a butterfly and wakes unsure which he is.

Both were written during the Warring States period, when Chinese kingdoms fought for supremacy and thinkers competed to advise them. Against the Confucian programme of ritual, study and moral effort, the Daoist texts proposed something quieter: return to simplicity, reduce desires, do not interfere, and trust the way things move of themselves.

From the second century of the common era Daoism also became an organised religion, with priests, temples, scriptures, a pantheon and communal rites. Alongside it grew arts of nourishing life: breathing, movement, diet and the meditative discipline called inner alchemy. Modern scholars no longer draw a hard line between a "philosophical" and a "religious" Daoism. They are two faces of one long tradition.

Its influence runs through Chinese medicine, landscape painting, poetry, garden design, the martial arts and tea. When Buddhism arrived in China it was first explained in Daoist words, and Chan, later Zen, carries the mark.

This Onda draws on the classics and on everyday practices anyone may do: gentle movement at dawn, an aimless walk, tea made slowly, time looking at the sky. Daoism is also a living religion with ordained clergy and its own rites. Those belong to its communities and are not imitated here.

figures.name: Laozi
figures.bio: The "Old Master", by legend a royal archivist who wrote the Tao Te Ching at a border pass before leaving China. Many scholars doubt he was a single historical person.

figures.name: Zhuangzi
figures.bio: Zhuang Zhou, a minor official who turned down high office. The Inner Chapters of the book that bears his name are among the great works of Chinese prose.

figures.name: Liezi
figures.bio: The sage who rode the wind. The book named for him was compiled centuries later.

figures.name: Zhang Daoling
figures.bio: Founder of the Way of the Celestial Masters, the first organised Daoist church.

figures.name: Wang Bi
figures.bio: A prodigy whose commentary shaped how the Tao Te Ching has been read ever since. He died at twenty-three.

figures.name: Ge Hong
figures.bio: Author of the Baopuzi, the Master Who Embraces Simplicity, on alchemy, immortals and ethics.

figures.name: Tao Yuanming
figures.bio: Poet who resigned his post to farm. The patron saint of going home.

figures.name: Wang Chongyang
figures.bio: Founder of the Quanzhen, Complete Perfection, school of monastic Daoism.

figures.name: Qiu Chuji
figures.bio: Quanzhen master who travelled to Central Asia to meet Genghis Khan and urged him to spare lives.

history.what: The Tao Te Ching takes shape
history.detail: The oldest surviving copies are bamboo slips buried around 300 BCE at Guodian. The text was probably compiled over time rather than written by one hand.
The seven Inner Chapters are generally thought to be his own. The rest of the book was added by followers and later editors.

history.what: Huang-Lao thought at the Han court
history.detail: Early Han rulers favoured a blend of Laozi and the Yellow Emperor: govern lightly and let the people recover from war.

history.what: The Way of the Celestial Masters is founded
history.detail: Zhang Daoling reported a revelation from the deified Laozi in Sichuan. His movement had parishes, registers and healing rites, and its lineage continues today.

history.what: The age of commentary and withdrawal
history.detail: Wang Bi writes on Laozi and Guo Xiang edits the Zhuangzi into the form we have. The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove make a point of drinking, music and avoiding office.
The fullest early account of the search for long life through alchemy, diet and virtue.
The medium Yang Xi records scriptures said to be dictated by celestial beings. The Highest Clarity school, centred on Mount Mao, turns Daoism toward inner visualisation.
The imperial family shared his surname, Li, and claimed him as an ancestor. Daoist texts entered the civil examinations and temples spread across the empire.
A celibate monastic order joining Daoist inner alchemy with Buddhist and Confucian elements. It is still one of the two main schools.
The seventy-four-year-old master travelled for two years to reach the khan’s camp near the Hindu Kush. Asked for the medicine of immortality, he said there was none, only ways to care for life.
The Ming Daozang gathers about fifteen hundred texts. It remains the standard collection.
The earliest reliable records place it in the Chen family village in Henan. The story of the immortal Zhang Sanfeng inventing it is later legend.
Silk copies of the Tao Te Ching from a tomb sealed in 168 BCE come to light at Mawangdui, and the older bamboo slips at Guodian twenty years later.

concepts.text: The Way: the source and course of all things.
concepts.detail: The first line of the Tao Te Ching warns that the Way that can be spoken of is not the constant Way. It is called the mother of the ten thousand things, yet it does not rule them. It can be followed but not grasped.

concepts.text: The power or virtue of the Way as it appears in a particular thing.
concepts.detail: The second half of the book’s title. A person of deep de is compared to an infant: soft, whole and unafraid.
The sage acts without acting and so nothing is left undone. It describes skill so complete that effort disappears, and government so light that people say: we did it ourselves.
Humans follow earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Way, and the Way follows what is naturally so.

concepts.text: The two complementary aspects of everything.
concepts.detail: Originally the shady and sunny sides of a hill. They are not good and evil. Each grows from the other, and health, in a body or a state, is their balance.

concepts.text: The breath or energy of which everything is made.
concepts.detail: Condensed it is matter, rarefied it is spirit. Movement, breathing and meditation practices all work with qi.
An image of the mind before preference and ambition have shaped it. To return to it is not to become ignorant but to become whole.

concepts.text: What is absent is what makes a thing work.
concepts.detail: The hollow of the cup, the space in the room, the pause in the music. Daoist texts keep directing attention to what is not there.

concepts.text: The arts of health and long life.
concepts.detail: Breathing, stretching, moderation in food and sex, and regular hours. Their heirs are qigong, tai chi and much of Chinese medicine.

concepts.text: Meditation as the refining of essence, breath and spirit.
concepts.detail: Neidan borrowed the vocabulary of the laboratory, furnace, cauldron and elixir, for a contemplative practice aimed at returning to the Way.

facts.text: The Tao Te Ching is among the most translated books in the world, with hundreds of versions in English alone.
In the Mawangdui manuscripts the two halves of the book are in the opposite order, De before Dao.
Laozi means "Old Master". By legend he was carried in his mother’s womb for decades and was born with white hair.
Gunpowder was discovered by Chinese alchemists looking for an elixir of long life.
The guqin piece Flowing Water travels on the Voyager Golden Record, launched in 1977.
Zhuangzi is said to have drummed on a bowl and sung after his wife died, explaining that she had only moved on with the seasons.
The yin-yang diagram familiar today is far younger than the idea. Its present form dates from around the Song and Ming dynasties.
The White Cloud Temple in Beijing, seat of the Quanzhen order, has been a Daoist site since the Tang dynasty.

glossary.meaning: The Classic of the Way and its Power. Also written Daodejing.
The first seven chapters of the Zhuangzi.
The oldest Daoist religious lineage, also called Zhengyi.
Complete Perfection: the monastic school founded in the twelfth century.
The period from about 475 to 221 BCE in which the classics were written.

learnFrom.name: A Daoist temple near you
learnFrom.note: Visit quietly, follow the customs of the place, and ask before taking photographs.

learnFrom.name: A qualified tai chi or qigong teacher
learnFrom.note: Movement is best learned in person, and many teachers hold classes in public parks.

sensitivity.note: Daoism is a living religion as well as a body of classic texts. This Onda uses the classics and common health practices. Priestly rites and initiations belong to Daoist communities and are not imitated here.
requiredCaveats: Qigong and tai chi are gentle, but stop if you feel dizzy or unwell.
Popular Western books on the Tao often leave out the religion. Read them alongside a scholarly or practitioner source.
